title: 'The Low-Threshold Mechanoreceptors: One Touch, Several Signals'

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What makes a cutaneous sensory neuron a low-threshold mechanoreceptor (LTMR)?
cards.back: It responds to mechanical stimulation too light to hurt.
cards.quote: A low-threshold mechanoreceptor (LTMR) is a cutaneous sensory neuron activated by touch too light to hurt
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: The slowly adapting touch afferent that reports a held indentation and its edges ends at {{c1::Merkel cells}}.
cards.back: Human SA I; mouse Aβ SA1, at Merkel cell-neurite complexes.
cards.quote: A slowly adapting afferent ending at Merkel cells (SA I) fires as the probe goes in and keeps firing while it is held.
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: Which end organ serves rapidly adapting Aβ RA1 afferents in glabrous skin, and what part of a press do they report?
cards.back: The Meissner corpuscle; they report skin motion at onset and sometimes at offset, with silence during the hold.
cards.why: Meissner afferents are most sensitive near 40 to 60 Hz; this is a band of best sensitivity, not a cutoff.
cards.quote: A rapidly adapting afferent ending in a Meissner corpuscle (RA) fires while the skin moves
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: Why do the labels rapidly adapting and slowly adapting describe a test response rather than everything a touch neuron encodes?
cards.back: They describe firing during a held step: rapid afferents fire at onset and sometimes offset; slow afferents keep firing. Natural movement contains more than a held step.
cards.quote: A step response does not tell you everything a neuron reports during natural movement.
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: How do Merkel-associated SA I and Pacinian (Aβ RA2) afferents provide complementary reports of the same contact?
cards.back: SA I maintains a report of held pressure and edges; Pacinian afferents detect tiny fast vibrations and are silent during the hold.
cards.quote: They show that the recorded classes are complementary: SA I afferents keep signalling a held press, while Pacinian afferents detect fast vibrations
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: A resting fingertip contact begins vibrating at an illustrative 180 Hz with tiny movements. Which class should detect the weakest vibration, and why?
cards.back: Pacinian (Aβ RA2) afferents should detect it best: 180 Hz lies within their band of greatest sensitivity, about 100 to 300 Hz.
cards.quote: It is the most sensitive of the classes to fast vibration, best near 100 to 300 Hz
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: A cutaneous afferent fires to both a feather-light touch and a painful pinch. Does the pinch response disqualify it as an LTMR, and why?
cards.back: No. Its response to innocuous touch establishes the low threshold; that designation does not impose an upper limit on the forces that can drive it.
cards.quote: An LTMR can fire to a pinch; what makes it an LTMR is that it also fires to a touch too light to hurt.
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: What determines which part of a touch an afferent favors, and what determines how fast its report travels?
cards.back: The end organ and the neuron's channels and excitability shape tuning. Axon diameter and myelin set conduction speed.
cards.why: The fibre groups Aβ, Aδ and C summarize speeds; a class's best stimulus and its conduction speed describe different properties.
cards.quote: Its end organ, together with the neuron's own channels and excitability, shapes which part.
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: A strong vibration drives a touch afferent outside its band of best sensitivity. Is that inconsistent with frequency tuning, and why?
cards.back: No. Best-sensitivity bands are not cutoffs; sufficiently strong vibrations can drive other classes too.
cards.quote: These are bands of best sensitivity, not cutoffs: a strong enough vibration drives other classes too.
cards.section: One press, several reports

cards.front: How does a lanceolate ending run relative to a hair follicle, compared with a circumferential ending?
cards.back: A lanceolate branch runs lengthwise, parallel to the hair shaft; a circumferential ending wraps around the follicle.
cards.quote: A lanceolate ending is an axon branch that runs lengthwise along a hair follicle, parallel to the shaft
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: A terminal Schwann cell is a {{c1::non-neuronal}} cell whose processes interleave with lanceolate endings.
cards.quote: A terminal Schwann cell is a non-neuronal cell whose processes interleave with lanceolate endings.
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: Which mouse LTMR class has circumferential endings around many follicles, and what stimulus best drives it?
cards.back: Aβ field-LTMRs; a stroke over a wide area.
cards.quote: Field-LTMRs, tuned to a stroke over a wide area, should answer too.
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: In the model of Abraira and Ginty (2013), why is mouse touch coding described as an ensemble rather than one labelled line per sensation?
cards.back: The stimulus recruits a combination of classes with different sensitivities. The nervous system reads their joint activity because no class reports the whole touch.
cards.quote: which classes fire depends on the stimulus, and touch is read from these ensembles of impulses from physiologically distinct LTMRs
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: In the reported mouse Aδ-LTMR threshold below 0.07 mN, what does the force refer to?
cards.back: A von Frey force: a calibrated filament is pressed until it bends. These afferents are highly sensitive to tiny hair deflections.
cards.why: The class table gives mouse Aδ-LTMRs a mean conduction velocity of 5.8 ± 0.9 m/s and rapid step adaptation, with lanceolate endings at awl/auchene and zigzag hairs.
cards.quote: The Aδ threshold is a von Frey force, set by a calibrated filament pressed until it bends.
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: What conduction velocity and step-adaptation pattern were reported for mouse C-LTMRs in the class table?
cards.back: 0.58 ± 0.02 m/s in that sample, with intermediate adaptation; their lanceolate endings respond to gentle deformation of hairy skin.
cards.quote: in the mouse, C-LTMRs conduct about ten times more slowly than Aδ-LTMRs.
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: Mouse hairy-skin means are 13.6 ± 2.7 m/s for Aβ RA1 and 17.0 ± 2.0 m/s for field-LTMRs. Why is speed alone a poor classifier?
cards.back: These are sample summaries, not class boundaries. Their means are close; distinguishing the classes requires response properties and endings as well as speed.
cards.quote: The two Aβ classes with mouse values, Aβ RA1 and field, have means only 3.4 m/s apart
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: A feather sweeps across mouse back skin, displacing hairs without compressing touch domes. Which LTMRs should respond most, and why?
cards.back: Aβ RA, Aδ and C hair afferents, plus field-LTMRs, should respond. SA1 responses should be small because hair displacement alone scarcely indents their touch domes.
cards.quote: they respond to indentation of the dome, not to deflection of the hair alone
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: A probe holds a mouse guard hair's touch dome indented after the skin stops moving. Which afferent should continue firing, and why?
cards.back: The Merkel-associated Aβ SA1 afferent should continue: its sustained response reports the indentation. Other classes can still respond during entry and withdrawal.
cards.quote: A held poke aimed at a guard hair's touch dome would reverse the picture, driving its SA1 afferents through the hold
cards.section: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table

cards.front: A genetic reporter marks a group of skin sensory neurons. Why must investigators record their responses before treating the label as an LTMR class?
cards.back: Gene expression supplies a label, not a functional classification. Recording must confirm the response properties of the labelled neurons.
cards.quote: A label is a handle, not a class, until physiology confirms it.
cards.section: The key experiment: label, record, map

cards.front: What is the dominant lanceolate-ending combination at mouse zigzag follicles, and how strictly should that map be read?
cards.back: Aδ- and C-LTMR endings occur in virtually all examined zigzag follicles; very few Aβ RA associations were also reported.
cards.quote: Zigzag: Aδ and C lanceolate endings, in virtually all follicles examined.
cards.section: The key experiment: label, record, map

cards.front: Which two LTMR arrangements characterize mouse guard hairs in the dominant follicle map?
cards.back: Aβ RA lanceolate endings along the follicle and Merkel-associated Aβ SA1 endings in the adjacent touch dome.
cards.quote: Guard: Aβ RA lanceolate endings, plus Merkel-associated Aβ SA1 endings in the touch dome beside the hair.
cards.section: The key experiment: label, record, map

cards.front: A mouse awl/auchene hair is jiggled and then held at its new angle. If all three lanceolate LTMR classes respond, how should their hold responses differ, and why?
cards.back: Aβ RA and Aδ units should fall quiet once movement stops; C-LTMRs should continue for part of the hold. Their adaptation patterns differ despite sharing the follicle.
cards.quote: The rapidly adapting Aβ RA and Aδ units fire as the hair moves and fall quiet in the hold; the C unit, with intermediate adaptation
cards.section: The key experiment: label, record, map

cards.front: Three sensory axons initiate spikes together over equal 2.0 cm paths at constant 13.6, 5.8 and 0.58 m/s. Ignoring initiation delays, calculate their arrival times.
cards.back: Use t = L/v with L = 0.020 m. Times are 0.020/13.6 ≈ 1.5 ms, 0.020/5.8 ≈ 3.4 ms and 0.020/0.58 ≈ 34 ms, respectively.
cards.quote: Take an illustrative 2.0 cm path, Li's mean velocities, constant speed and conduction alone.
cards.section: The key experiment: label, record, map

cards.front: Two sensory fibres have known velocities and equal path lengths, but unknown spike-initiation delays. Can conduction calculations alone predict their measured first-spike latency gap? Explain.
cards.back: No. The rule t = L/v predicts conduction time, whereas measured response latency also depends on when each spike starts. Equal paths and known velocities do not establish simultaneous initiation.
cards.quote: These are conduction times, not measured response latencies.
cards.section: The key experiment: label, record, map

cards.front: Why does counting the follicles contacted by sensory afferents fail to give a neuron count?
cards.back: One afferent branches to many follicles, so multiple follicle contacts can belong to the same neuron.
cards.quote: a single afferent branches to many follicles, so a count of endings at hairs is not a count of neurons.
cards.section: The key experiment: label, record, map

cards.front: What are human C-tactile (CT) afferents?
cards.back: Unmyelinated afferents responding to gentle deformation, recorded in forearm hairy skin; they are physiologically similar to mouse C-LTMRs.
cards.quote: recorded unmyelinated afferents in human forearm hairy skin that respond to gentle deformation, the C-tactile (CT) afferents, physiologically similar to mouse C-LTMRs.
cards.section: Your own skin: human touch classes and C-tactile afferents

cards.front: A human touch afferent is classified from its firing and receptive field. Why does that classification alone fail to identify its anatomical ending?
cards.back: The recording measures physiology, not ending anatomy. A firing-defined class requires separate anatomical evidence before assigning an end organ.
cards.why: Human RA, PC and SA I align by firing with mouse RA1, RA2 and SA1. The SA II ending remains unresolved; a Ruffini assignment is an inference.
cards.quote: The human classes rest on firing and receptive fields; no ending was seen.
cards.section: Your own skin: human touch classes and C-tactile afferents

cards.front: Within the brushing-speed range tested by Löken et al. (2009), how should human CT firing change relative to Aβ firing as a forearm brush accelerates, and why?
cards.back: CT firing should peak at about 1 to 10 cm/s, then fall as speed rises; Aβ firing should keep rising. The reported CT velocity curve is an inverted U.
cards.quote: CT firing followed an inverted U across brushing velocities, peaking at about 1 to 10 cm/s
cards.section: Your own skin: human touch classes and C-tactile afferents

cards.front: Why does a contribution of human C-tactile afferents to affective touch not make them a complete explanation of pleasant touch?
cards.back: Not all affective touch relies on CTs, and affective touch need not be pleasant. CTs contribute to affective touch rather than accounting for every experience.
cards.quote: not every affective touch relies on CTs, and affective touch need not be pleasant
cards.section: Your own skin: human touch classes and C-tactile afferents

cards.front: In adult mouse trunk skin, how does the side enriched in Aδ-LTMR endings differ from the preferred direction of hair movement?
cards.back: Endings are enriched on the caudal, tail side; preferred deflection is toward the head. How the arrangement produces that mechanical preference remains unknown.
cards.quote: The endings are mounted on the tail side; the neuron's preferred movement is the hair tip swinging toward the head.
cards.section: How a tuning is built: direction

cards.front: Mouse follicle epithelium lacks BDNF throughout development. What happens to the alignment of Aδ-LTMR hair-direction preferences, and why?
cards.back: Preferred directions become randomized relative to the body axis, with disrupted caudal ending polarity. Epithelial BDNF is required to organize those endings during development.
cards.quote: The caudal polarity of the endings was disrupted, and the neurons' preferred direction was randomized relative to the body axis.
cards.section: How a tuning is built: direction

cards.front: After developmental epithelial Bdnf deletion, mouse Aδ-LTMR direction preferences are disorganized. Which control distinguishes disorganization from neuron loss, and how should it be interpreted?
cards.back: Check Aδ-LTMR survival and general maturation. Their retention supports disorganized tuning rather than loss of the population. This rests on the rule that a changed response must be distinguished from absent neurons.
cards.quote: Aδ-LTMR survival and general maturation were retained.
cards.section: How a tuning is built: direction

cards.front: Developmental epithelial Bdnf deletion disrupts mouse Aδ-LTMR polarity. What further tests would separate an adult BDNF requirement from developmental organization and establish touch-evoked release?
cards.back: Use an adult inducible deletion to test adult function, and measure release during touch separately. The developmental perturbation establishes organization during development; it does not establish acute BDNF release.
cards.quote: Because the deletion acted through development, the result shows that epithelial BDNF is required to organize the endings, not that BDNF is released during touch.
cards.section: How a tuning is built: direction

cards.front: A marker labels candidate mouse SA2-like neurons. How would you link a sustained stretch response to their ending while keeping the human conclusion bounded?
cards.back: Record labelled neurons for innocuous threshold, conduction velocity, held-step firing and stretch response; then identify recorded endings anatomically. The label-record-map rule could establish a mouse class, but cannot identify human SA II endings.
cards.quote: Image whole mounts of labelled skin, and confirm the ending of recorded neurons afterwards
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Activating a sensory class evokes a behavior, while removing it leaves a reduced but persistent response to the natural stimulus. What combined causal conclusion follows?
cards.back: Activity in the class is sufficient to evoke the behavior, and the class contributes to the natural response. A partial loss does not establish an exclusive route; this follows from combining activation with incomplete behavioral loss.
cards.quote: optogenetic activation of C-LTMRs evoked wet dog shakes, and adult ablation cut oil-droplet-evoked shakes by about half
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: Why would finding the same ending shape in touch afferents fail to establish identical stimulus tuning?
cards.back: Ending type alone does not set tuning; the neuron's channels and excitability also matter. Shared ending morphology can accompany different thresholds and adaptation.
cards.quote: The ending type alone does not set the tuning.
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: A mouse LTMR velocity summary gives a mean ± value without identifying SD or SEM. Can its size establish a boundary for classifying single neurons? Why?
cards.back: No. Size alone does not identify SD versus SEM, and either summary describes a sample rather than a class boundary. Physiology and anatomy are still needed.
cards.quote: Either way, treat the values as summaries of these samples, not as boundaries between classes.
cards.section: Where the class-table numbers come from

cards.front: Three sensory classes report one skin movement, and tracing shows their central endings align in a spinal column. Can this anatomy establish how their different touch reports are combined? Explain.
cards.back: No. The rule is that anatomical alignment establishes organization, not the functional computation. Combining reports from distinct afferents remains a circuit question requiring functional evidence.
cards.quote: That alignment is anatomy; how the columns combine their inputs is the subject of dorsal horn touch.
cards.section: The dorsal horn columns

cards.front: An idealized mouse patch has 1 guard, 23 awl/auchene and 76 zigzag follicles. Count 2, 3 and 2 LTMR classes per follicle, respectively, excluding field-LTMRs and exceptions. How many class–follicle associations are present?
cards.back: Sum follicles × classes per follicle: (1 × 2) + (23 × 3) + (76 × 2) = 2 + 69 + 152 = 223 associations. This is not a neuron count.
cards.quote: count each class once per follicle it innervates, and leave out field-LTMRs and the rare exceptions.
cards.section: Counting follicle associations is not counting neurons

cards.front: A nerve-electrode survey detects a rare afferent less often in one skin region than another. Does the encounter ratio alone prove the same ratio of anatomical densities? Why?
cards.back: No. It supports a sampling-based estimate, not a direct anatomical census. The inference depends on how the electrode samples the afferents.
cards.quote: an estimate that rests on electrode sampling.
cards.section: Small human samples: palm CTs and friction

cards.front: A sensory neuron fires H = 12 spikes to hair deflection toward the head and T = 3 toward the tail. Using direction index = (H − T)/(H + T), calculate and interpret its preference.
cards.back: (12 − 3)/(12 + 3) = 9/15 = +0.60, a preference toward the head. Positive means head-preferring; negative means tail-preferring.
cards.quote: the head direction is fixed by the body axis, so a neuron tuned the other way gets a negative index
cards.section: Direction tuning in detail

cards.front: For direction index = (H − T)/(H + T), why must a trial with no spikes in either direction be distinguished from an index of zero?
cards.back: No spikes gives a zero denominator, so the index is undefined and the trial unresponsive. Zero index instead means equal nonzero responses in both directions.
cards.quote: direction index = (H − T) / (H + T), for H + T > 0
cards.section: Direction tuning in detail
